summary:
Corrientes Province stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world. Law 26.743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, promulgated on 24 May 2012, and permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010, the first Latin American country to do so, and anti-discrimination protection operates through a combination of national and provincial laws.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action binding every province, Corrientes included. Emergency Decree 62/2025, issued on 5 February 2025, amends the Gender Identity Law to bar people under 18 from gender-affirming surgery and comprehensive hormonal treatment. Decree 61/2025, issued the same period, governs the placement of transgender people in the prison system. The LGBTIQ+ legal organisation FALGBT announced legal action over both decrees and constitutional experts called them unlawful; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

The national government has also removed institutional protections that a trans visitor would previously have been able to rely on. Trans people hired under the 1% public-sector Trans Labor Quota were dismissed, and the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI was abolished.

Violence risk is the sharpest concern for a visitor. Activists interviewed in April 2025 reported that police violence, already common against trans and travesti sex workers, had worsened under the Milei government and is worst outside Buenos Aires. The Washington Blade report of 10 April 2025, dateline Buenos Aires, names Corrientes among the more conservative interior provinces where the situation is worse. The same report describes the national framework as binding all provinces.

Recorded hate-crime violence reached a high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio counted at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours; Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026 and called them an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

Protection machinery has weakened at the level of the courts as well. On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, but rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.

An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration despite the statute's text.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina's permissive statute and its current enforcement climate point in opposite directions, and a visitor should read both. Law 26.743 and the 2010 marriage equality law place Argentina ahead of most of its neighbours on paper, while an Outright International overview of 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, indicating deterioration over the period covered.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed on 4 April 2025 by the Washington Blade, including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins, said the national government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

Interior provinces are described as worse than the capital for police violence against trans and travesti sex workers, which places Corrientes on the higher-risk side of a national pattern rather than as an isolated case. The abolition of INADI removed the body that had handled discrimination complaints nationally, leaving provincial anti-discrimination laws as the remaining avenue.

The decrees on minors and on prison placement were challenged rather than accepted: FALGBT announced legal action and constitutional experts called them unlawful, with the litigation outcome unresolved in the sources available here.

Adults retain the full scope of Law 26.743, including legal gender change without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval.

Decree 61/2025 governs where transgender people are held in the prison system, a rule that applies in Corrientes correctional facilities as elsewhere in Argentina.

Trans residents who had obtained public-sector work under the 1% Trans Labor Quota were dismissed, and the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI no longer exists, so complaints of discrimination are directed to provincial mechanisms.

outOfScopeNotes:
The sources available here do not record the outcome of the litigation brought against Emergency Decree 62/2025 and Decree 61/2025, so whether the decrees survive constitutional challenge is unresolved.

No Corrientes-specific figures on hate crimes, police complaints or prosecutions are sourced; the 227 hate crimes recorded for 2025 by the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio are national, not provincial.

Whether Decree 61/2025 has been implemented in Corrientes prisons, and how trans detainees are actually housed there, is not sourced.

The basis for the negative assessments in the Outright International overview of 12 March 2026 is not detailed in the inventory, and the relationship between those assessments and the text of Law 26.743 is unresolved.

Access to gender-affirming care, ID document procedures and facilities at Corrientes points of entry are not covered by the sources available here.
